Please call 000 now if someone has been bitten by a snake or a funnel-web spider, or has trouble breathing, a swollen face or throat, or has collapsed. For other bites and stings, please call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 for advice, at any time of day. For a pet, please call your vet.

Please call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 now, even if there are no signs yet. It answers at any time of day, from anywhere in Australia. Please call 000 if the person is unconscious, has trouble breathing or is having a fit. For a pet, please call your vet or an emergency vet straight away, and take the plant or a photo of it with you.

Please never eat a plant, fruit, mushroom or animal because of an identification in this app, even one it is sure of. Many poisonous plants and mushrooms look like ones that are not. Please ask an expert who can see it in person first.

Please follow the product\'s label for how much to use and how to mix and apply it. The label also says what protective gear to wear and how long to wait before harvest. The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) registers these products, and its online register lists each one.

Please call the Exotic Plant Pest Hotline on 1800 084 881 if you think your bees have varroa mite or another exotic pest. American foulbrood, European foulbrood and other notifiable bee diseases are reported to your state\'s agriculture department. Please don\'t move hives, bees or equipment until you have spoken with them.

Please don\'t touch, pick up or try to move an animal that may be dangerous, and please keep children and pets away from it. An identification in this app never decides whether something is safe to handle. For a snake, please call a licensed snake catcher; your council can tell you who is licensed nearby. For a wasp nest or a bee swarm, please call a licensed pest controller or a local beekeeper.

Until then, please keep it somewhere warm, dark and quiet, and please don\'t give it food or water. Please don\'t touch a bat or flying-fox at all, because they can carry lyssavirus.

Remind me to check for mites every month

The Biosecurity Code of Practice asks for each hive\'s brood to be checked for pests and disease at least three times a year, at least three months apart. It asks for a mite check every month, all year, where Varroa is established and the hive has brood. Elsewhere, it asks for at least one hive in each apiary to be checked for mites in spring, summer and autumn.
Queensland asks beekeepers to check their hives for Varroa mite every month, and to report every check on its Bee 123 form, even when no mites are found.

Sunken or perforated cappings, ropy brood and twisted larvae can be signs of American or European foulbrood. American foulbrood must be reported in every state and territory, and European foulbrood everywhere except Queensland. Please contact your state or territory\'s department of agriculture, and please keep the hive\'s frames and equipment away from your other hives until you have spoken with them.

Seen on it in your yard

No birds have been recorded this year. Dense or prickly shrubs give small birds shelter, a shallow bath out of a cat\'s reach gives them water, and native plants that flower at different times feed honeyeaters through the year.
No insects have been recorded this year. Flowers through the year, a patch of bare ground or a bee hotel to nest in, and no sprays while plants are flowering bring bees, butterflies and hover flies.

No frogs have been recorded this year. A pond or bog garden that holds water for weeks, with shallow edges, plants around it and no fish, gives them somewhere to breed. Snail pellets and sprays harm them.

No reptiles have been recorded this year. Rocks and logs in a sunny spot to bask on, with leaf litter, mulch and low plants to hide in, suit skinks and blue-tongued lizards. Snail pellets harm them too.
